text: Every lock type you've learned so far has to be taken on something. That something can be a different size, and this lesson is about those sizes: row, page, and table locking.

A row lock covers a single row — the most granular option. A page lock covers an 8KB page, typically holding several rows together. And a table lock covers the entire table at once — the least granular.

These trade off in opposite directions. Row locks give the best concurrency — two transactions on different rows never conflict — but tracking thousands of individual row locks has real memory and CPU cost. Table locks have almost no tracking overhead, one entry regardless of how many rows are touched, but the worst concurrency: nothing else can touch any row in that table, even ones the holder never looked at. Page locks sit in between.

In practice, a targeted single-row UPDATE typically gets a row lock, cheap to track and narrowly scoped. A bulk UPDATE touching a large fraction of the table might instead get page or table-level locking, trading some concurrency for far less overhead.

You don't pick this directly in ordinary T-SQL. SQL Server's query optimizer chooses the granularity automatically, based on cost estimates: how many rows a statement is expected to touch, the table and index structure, and current conditions.

And the optimizer's up-front choice isn't the whole story. A statement that starts with row locks can still escalate to a full table lock partway through if it crosses a certain threshold — and that's exactly what the next lesson covers.
